item.title: China’s clean-tech exports to Southeast Asia surge despite regional tensions
item.description:
Source: The Economist - China Original headline: China’s exports of clean tech to South-East Asia are soaring
China's clean-tech exports to Southeast Asia have surged, outpacing European demand. Unlike the EU, where governments fret over competition, Southeast Asian nations show little concern. The Iran war disrupted oil supplies, spurring demand for cheaper energy. The Philippines, now the world’s second-largest buyer of Chinese solar panels, faces long installation waits. Trade group member Ping Mendoza notes delays of two to three months. Despite territorial disputes with China, the Philippines prioritizes energy security over security concerns. Southeast Asia also repackages Chinese tech for Western markets, evading tariffs. China’s solar exports to the region rose 60% in nine months, while European sales dropped 11%. Countries like Laos and Malaysia are promoting clean energy, with Indonesia aiming to expand solar capacity to 100GW by 2029. Colin Steley, an Australian energy seller in the Philippines, highlights the region’s focus on rapid renewable expansion. Chinese firms are meeting this demand.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Rise Slightly to 7.09% Today
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Thursday, November 12: A Little Higher
Mortgage rates rose slightly today to 7.09% APR for a 30-year fixed-rate loan, up 9 basis points from yesterday and 13 basis points from a week ago. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported 0.4% inflation in October, exceeding forecasts of 0.3%. The Federal Reserve may raise interest rates again in December and possibly January as inflation remains above its 2% target. Refinancing could be beneficial if current rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 percentage points lower than existing rates, though lenders adjust pricing frequently. Homebuyers are advised to lock rates if satisfied with a quote, especially with float-down options. Rates can fluctuate daily, and personalized quotes depend on credit scores, down payments, and other financial factors. Preapproval and comparing offers are recommended to navigate current market conditions.

item.title: German Robotics Firm Valued at $8.5 Billion After $500 Million Investment
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business Original headline: Tech Giants Invest in German Robotics Start-Up at $8.5 Billion Valuation
Agile Robots, a German industrial robotics firm, secured $500 million in funding from SoftBank, Nvidia, and others, valuing the company at $8.5 billion. Founder Zhaopeng Chen said the investment will enable expansion in the U.S., increased production in Germany, and entry into new markets ahead of a potential IPO. Agile, which partners with Google DeepMind, has raised $2 billion total and deployed 30,000 robotics systems, including 3,000-4,000 humanoids, across automotive, electronics, and logistics sectors. The company aims to double sales to 600 million euros this year. Chen highlighted Europe’s push to close an AI gap with the U.S. and China, noting the region’s slow progress. Agile’s valuation rivals European firms like Quantum Systems ($8 billion) and Wayve ($8.6 billion). Challenges include ensuring reliable AI robot operation, with companies like Hexagon Robotics testing systems at BMW’s Leipzig plant. Chen emphasized Europe’s need to adapt, citing China’s 2.3 million industrial robots and Unitree’s 460% stock surge. He argued Europe still has a chance in the new era of physical AI.

item.title: United Airlines Blocks A.I. Agents From Booking Flights
item.description:
Source: NYT > Business
United Airlines is banning artificial intelligence agents from booking flights or accessing user accounts, citing privacy risks and potential regulatory violations. The airline warned that AI agents could expose personal data, cause unintended purchases, or alter account details without human oversight. It highlighted flight check-in as a task requiring human confirmation to ensure bags do not contain banned items. The move follows concerns about AI agents acting independently, such as an incident where an Anthropic model submitted a fake homicide tip to police. Meta, Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic have developed AI assistants capable of completing tasks like booking reservations. United Airlines stated it will review AI use as the technology evolves, prioritizing customer protection. The companies did not immediately comment on the airline’s decision.

item.title: Nvidia CEO Resigns Amid National Security Concerns and Affair Scandal
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune, Business Insider, BBC News, The Atlantic, NYT > Business, The New York Times, FT World, FT News Feed, The Economist - Business
Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a spy for Beijing. The board, which had investigated whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence, announced his departure, ending his 33-year tenure. Huang’s resignation followed media reports of an affair with an Nvidia employee, per The New York Times. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO since 2013, became interim CEO, stating the company’s strength lies in its people. The board also named Harvey C. Jones as chairman. Nvidia shares fell 14% at open, later dropping 4.2%, with the stock down 32% from its October peak, eroding $1.8 trillion in value. U.S. lawmakers demanded answers about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang and security protocols. Rep. Brian Mast threatened subpoenas, while the FBI investigates. President Trump praised Huang’s leadership. Analysts warn the lack of a succession plan could disrupt Nvidia’s role in the AI boom, which relies on its chips for 90% of advanced AI projects. The scandal has intensified scrutiny of Nvidia’s ties to Megaspeed, accused of shipping chips to China. Singaporean authorities confirmed they questioned Alice Huang and seized documents. The tech industry awaits Nvidia’s next leadership steps amid uncertainty about its future.
item.source: San Diego Union-Tribune, Business Insider, BBC News, The Atlantic, NYT > Business, The New York Times, FT World, FT News Feed, The Economist - Business

item.title: New Brain Atlas Reveals Disease-Linked Cells and Therapies
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: New brain atlas promises disease breakthroughs
Scientists created the largest multi-species brain atlas of the basal ganglia, a region vital for movement, emotions, and decision-making. The research, involving over 500 scientists across nine countries, identified a new nerve cell type linked to schizophrenia risk, a modified gene therapy for Parkinson’s that reduces tremors in animals, and genetic connections between basal ganglia cells and autism. The atlas profiles 25.5 million cells from humans, macaques, marmosets, and mice, using advanced gene activity analysis. Evan Macosko of Harvard Medical School called the atlas a foundational map for understanding and treating neurological disorders. Hongkui Zeng of the Allen Institute emphasized the need for precise cell-type analysis to study disease mechanisms. Researchers also found aging patterns tied to gene activity across cell types. Frank Hirth of King’s College London described the basal ganglia as essential for motor control and sensory awareness. Scientists noted the work provides a roadmap for future studies, though further validation of molecular findings is needed to determine causal relationships and therapeutic potential.

item.title: American Cancer Society Recommends Universal Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Ages 50-69
item.description:
Source: The New York Times, Washington Post
The American Cancer Society updated prostate cancer screening guidelines, recommending universal blood tests every two years for men aged 50-69. Black men and those with a strong family history should start annual screening at 45. This replaces prior advice emphasizing shared decision-making. The guidelines cite a European study of 160,000 men showing 13% reduced prostate cancer mortality over 23 years, with two deaths averted per 1,000 screened. The PSA test detects elevated levels but requires follow-up imaging or biopsies. Critics warn of overdiagnosis risks, including unnecessary procedures like biopsies, radiation, or surgery, which can cause side effects. The ACS contrasts its recommendations with the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force’s previous stance against routine testing. The guidelines also address disparities, urging earlier screening for high-risk groups. Dr. William Dahut emphasized balancing early detection with overdiagnosis risks, while Dr. Alex Krist cautioned against widespread screening without individual risk assessments. The ACS acknowledges challenges in implementation and stresses patient-doctor discussions for informed choices.
item.source: The New York Times, Washington Post

item.title: UK economy grows 0.7% in third quarter, fastest since 2024
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: UK economy expanded by 0.7% in third quarter
UK economy expanded by 0.7% in the third quarter, the fastest growth since 2024, driven by the services sector, particularly IT and AI-related activities. The Office for National Statistics reported the increase, matching economist expectations, with services growing 0.9% and manufacturing up 0.9%. Construction output fell 0.7%. George Brown of Schroders noted the economy’s resilience despite energy costs and borrowing costs. The Bank of England warned of inflationary pressures, forecasting 5% inflation next year and potential further rate hikes. Annual growth in Q3 was 1.9% compared to a year earlier. The BoE raised rates to 4% and upgraded 2026 growth forecasts to 1.6%, though 2027 growth is expected to slow to 1.3%. Matt Swannell highlighted the narrow base of growth, with AI adoption boosting IT services but falling incomes straining consumer sectors. Swaps markets suggest a 75% chance of another rate hike in December. The pound remained stable, and the Treasury praised the growth as the strongest in nearly a decade outside the pandemic. Chancellor John Healey credited resilience amid the Middle East conflict.

item.title: Wizz Air CEO urges EU-wide action against bomb threats
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Wizz Air chief calls for Europe-wide response to bomb hoaxes
Wizz Air CEO József Váradi urged European authorities to adopt a unified approach to address hoax bomb threats after over 50 flights across the region were targeted last week, including 14 involving his airline. He criticized the absence of a coordinated European response, stating national security is treated as a sovereign matter. Flights were diverted, military jets scrambled, and one aircraft landed at a military base. Váradi emphasized the need for improved European cooperation, while ACI Europe’s Olivier Jankovec highlighted gaps in current security frameworks. The airline reported a 66% drop in pre-tax profits for the six months ending September, driven by fuel costs, though summer performance exceeded expectations. Váradi noted rising costs from aircraft deals and warned of potential winter price hikes.

item.title: Kenya Ends Ebola Outbreak After Last Patient Discharged
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: Kenya Starts Countdown to End of Ebola Outbreak
Kenya's Ebola outbreak is nearing an end after the last patient was discharged from the hospital. Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale announced that no active cases or quarantined contacts remain, marking the first time since the outbreak began that Kenya has zero patients or contacts. The final patient, a Kenyan man who contracted the virus from a Congolese source, died days after isolation. Nine total cases and two deaths were recorded in Kenya, all linked to the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Authorities confirmed no community transmission occurred, as all infected individuals were in quarantine before symptoms developed. The outbreak will be officially declared over on Dec. 23 if no new cases emerge. Globally, the outbreak has killed over 5,300 people since May, but spread beyond Africa has not materialized. Uganda and Nigeria contained their outbreaks by August and last month, respectively. Travel restrictions, including the U.S. CDC's 21-day quarantine rule for travelers from Congo, have been implemented. Kenya will enforce 21 days of quarantine for returning citizens from Congo, though details on location remain unspecified.

item.title: US Army Funds AI Drones to Detect Threats and Protect Abrams Tanks
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: The US Army is putting money on AI drones that can find hidden threats and protect its Abrams tanks
The US Army has awarded a $2.5 million contract to Safe Pro Group to integrate its Ground Truth threat-detection software into Anduril Industries' Ghost-X drone. The software, trained on Ukrainian battlefield data, identifies over 150 explosive threats and enemy drones from aerial imagery. It aims to protect Abrams tanks by mapping land mines, anti-personnel mines, cluster munitions, and first-person-view ambush drones. The contract reflects the Army's shift in tactics amid evolving threats like aerial drones and ground robots. Ukrainian battlefields highlight risks such as minefields and FPV drones, forcing armored units to adopt cautious approaches. Ghost-X drones will use AI to detect threats and share data via military networks like ATAK and Lattice. Daniel Leighton of Anduril noted the technology enhances situational awareness, supporting tank survivability and reconnaissance missions.

item.title: Community Colleges Expand Semiconductor Training to Address Labor Shortage
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Community colleges rush to expand semiconductor training as labor shortage looms US chip industry
Community colleges are expanding semiconductor training programs to address a looming labor shortage in the U.S. chip industry. The 2022 CHIPS Act, which allocates $800 billion for new semiconductor plants, has spurred partnerships between federal agencies, companies like TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix, and community colleges. Programs like Rio Salado College’s free, 12-week semiconductor manufacturing course offer hands-on training in clean-room labs, with students learning fabrication procedures via VR and practical skills in labs. Over 200 colleges nationwide now collaborate with SEMI to prepare workers for new plants. Shari Liss of SEMI warns of a potential 157,000 worker shortage by 2030, with Texas, Ohio, and Arizona facing the most acute gaps. Programs aim to fill entry-level roles quickly, with 75% of Rio Salado graduates securing semiconductor jobs. Companies also bring in experienced engineers from Asia to support U.S. plants, while emphasizing the need for precision and safety in training. Ethan Mock, a student in the program, highlights the opportunity to enter a booming industry without accumulating debt, as new facilities like TSMC’s $265 billion Arizona plant create thousands of jobs.

item.title: Instacart Expands to Deliver Non-Alcoholic Supplies to Bars and Restaurants
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Instacart wants to deliver supplies to your favorite bar or restaurant
Instacart has partnered with Provi, a B2B alcohol marketplace, to offer same-day delivery of non-alcoholic supplies like mixers and paper products to bars and restaurants. The collaboration excludes alcohol due to U.S. three-tier distribution laws. Provi CEO Matthew Tucker said the partnership addresses last-minute stock shortages, such as extra limes or napkins. Instacart's Andrew Nodes noted the service helps establishments operate smoothly during peak times. The partnership launches ahead of Thanksgiving and Christmas, Provi's busiest periods. Non-alcoholic items, including high-margin garnishes, are critical for sales, Tucker added. Labor shortages in the hospitality sector further drive demand for quick restocking. Provi users will order via its platform and redirect to Instacart for purchases. The move expands Instacart's B2B offerings beyond individual shoppers, targeting businesses like resorts and ice cream brands.

item.title: SS United States Sunk as Largest Artificial Reef Off Florida Coast
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News, BBC News Original headline: SS United States Sunk as World's Largest Artificial Reef Off Florida Coast
The SS United States, the world's fastest ocean liner and longest ship ever built, was sunk off Florida's coast on Wednesday to become the Gulf of Mexico's largest artificial reef. The 1,000-foot vessel, which held the trans-Atlantic speed record since 1952, was deliberately lowered 180 feet underwater in an upright position after 18 months of preparation. Okaloosa County, Florida, purchased the ship in 2024 and worked with Coleen Marine to execute the project, ensuring it sank straight down without explosives. The ship's original structure was preserved to maintain its recognizable form. Notable passengers included Harry Truman, Walt Disney, Marilyn Monroe, and young Bill Clinton. Retired in 1969, the ship spent decades docked in Philadelphia before being moved to Alabama for restoration. Legal and financial hurdles prevented its preservation as a museum or hotel, leading to its sale. Coleen Marine President Coleen O'Malley emphasized the hull's preservation. A land-based museum will detail its history. The ship, which could have been a military transport, now serves as a marine habitat and symbol of human ingenuity.

item.title: Nvidia's Leadership Changes After Jensen Huang Resigns
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Read the memos sent to Nvidia employees after Jensen Huang's resignation
Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones addressed employees Thursday after founder Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs. Kress announced a company meeting on November 18 to discuss the company's future, while Jones stated the board is seeking a permanent CEO from internal and external candidates. In internal memos, Kress emphasized employee resilience and the company's role in the AI revolution, pledging continued support. Jones highlighted Huang's legacy as a tech pioneer and expressed confidence in Kress's leadership, noting her role in shaping Nvidia's growth. Both leaders reaffirmed commitment to shareholders, customers, and employees, stressing the company's strength in its workforce and technological innovation. The board has no immediate timeline for selecting a new CEO.

item.title: One dead in E. coli outbreak tied to California pumpkin farm
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: One dead in E. coli outbreak linked to California pumpkin farm
One person died in an E. coli outbreak linked to Brookshire Farms in San Luis Obispo County. Health officials confirmed the death Tuesday, citing laboratory-confirmed infections in five individuals. Over a dozen people who visited the farm in late October reported symptoms, including three children requiring pediatric intensive care. Testing of farm samples did not identify the specific E. coli strain, and the exact source remains undetermined. The farm temporarily closed during peak season, with co-owner Shawn Callaway expressing devastation over the outbreak. The city canceled its Pumpkin Smash event due to concerns. Health officials stated there is no ongoing public health threat. Shiga toxin-producing E. coli cases in California rose from around 500 in 2011 to over 2,500 in 2023, according to state records.

item.title: European Schools Targeted by Bomb Hoax in Cyber Campaign
item.description:
Source: BBC News, FP Foreign Policy Original headline: Bomb Hoax Threatens European Schools in Suspected Hybrid Warfare Campaign
Schools in Italy, Scotland, and Northern Ireland received bomb threats via email, prompting evacuations but no explosives found. Over 6,300 Italian state schools and hundreds in Scotland and Northern Ireland received anonymous warnings signed by 'Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan.' Italian officials confirmed the threats originated from a single email sent to 6,300 schools, with similar messages reaching Scottish institutions. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the incidents part of a 'strategy to cause alarm,' while Scottish education secretary Mairi McAllan denied public risk. The threats were linked to broader cyberattacks, including false bomb warnings at airports and hacking of supermarkets and blood banks. Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara called the attacks a 'cyber-attack, not a genuine risk,' citing hybrid warfare tactics. Officials suspect Russia or Iran, citing past incidents like a drone attack on Germany’s airport and a refrigeration system hack in France. French authorities accused Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of a supermarket attack. Emails originated from hacked accounts in the Philippines and Taiwan. Protests erupted in Rome after a headmaster failed to evacuate, with some parents keeping children home. The Italian government warns threats may continue as part of a broader disruption effort.

item.title: Ukraine Reports Starlink Restrictions Amid US-Moscow Talks
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: Ukraine says Starlink restrictions are back as US envoys land in Moscow
Ukraine reported renewed speed restrictions on Starshield, the Pentagon-funded Starlink military service, hindering efforts to intercept Russian drones. President Zelenskyy accused Russia of imposing the limits to pressure Kyiv during peace talks, calling the restrictions 'helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians.' The service, limited to 161kph (100mph) over Ukraine’s front line and occupied territory, was previously disrupted last month, with Musk and the Trump administration blaming each other. Zelenskyy’s office sought clarification from Washington, which remained silent. The European Commission called the restrictions 'unacceptable' and urged SpaceX to restore services. Meanwhile, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Putin in Moscow, with Russia insisting on territorial demands for a peace deal. Putin emphasized 'eternal' peace but warned that 'grey zones' would destabilize agreements, demanding Kyiv withdraw from occupied regions. Russia’s negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, proposed a new European security system, framing it as a replacement for post-WWII order. European leaders expressed concern over Russia’s influence on security architecture discussions.

item.title: British Woman Missing From Atlantic Cruise Ship
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: British woman missing from cruise ship in Atlantic
A British woman went missing from Tui's Marella Voyager cruise ship while crossing the Atlantic. The 72-year-old was last seen on Monday and reported missing on Tuesday when crew noticed her bed unoccupied. The US Coast Guard instructed the ship to continue its route to the Caribbean rather than reverse for a search. Passengers were asked to abandon activities as crew conducted an emergency headcount. The UK Foreign Office confirmed support for the family. The Marella Voyager, carrying 2,000 passengers, is en route to Antigua. A spokeswoman for Marella Cruises expressed condolences and stated the company would not comment further. Separately, a Royal Caribbean pianist was found treading water 20 miles off California after falling overboard, believed to have spent nine hours in the water. The US Coast Guard issued an alert for the missing woman, urging nearby ships to assist in the search.

item.title: Millennials Had Easier Homebuying in 20s, Now Face Higher Costs
item.description:
Source: Washington Post Original headline: Which generation has had it easiest for homebuying? New research shows a shift.
Redfin economists compared homebuying conditions for millennials and boomers, finding millennials had easier access in their 20s and 30s due to lower interest rates and higher incomes. However, post-pandemic price and rate spikes have made mortgage payments for older millennials significantly higher than for boomers at a similar life stage. Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research, noted that millennials who bought before the pandemic fared well, but those entering the market afterward faced a tougher climate. The analysis tracked hypothetical mortgage payments for a median-priced home based on age, showing the post-pandemic rate spike disproportionately affected millennials in their late 30s. Boomers bought during periods of high rates but lower prices, with opportunities to refinance. Millennials, however, face higher prices and cannot refinance, making their initial advantage less sustainable. Factors like two-career households and student loans further strain millennial buyers. Zhao argued that millennials’ perception of a worse deal stems from later economic shifts, not an accurate comparison of their parents’ early experiences.

item.title: States revive asset seizures in economic warfare
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: The return of the snatch-and-grab state
A new book by Nicholas Mulder of Cornell University traces the history of state confiscation, from World War I to modern economic warfare. During the 1917-1918 war, A. Mitchell Palmer’s office seized German-owned assets in the U.S., auctioning them to fund the war effort. By 1918, Germany had lost over half its foreign assets. Today, Western nations have blocked $60bn in Russian oligarch assets and frozen $300bn in central-bank reserves since 2022. Debates persist over using seized funds, with Belgium fearing liability and Christine Lagarde warning of breaking international law. Mulder notes confiscation has long been tied to state power, with Grotius’ 17th-century theory of eminent domain shaping modern systems. Confiscation resurged in post-colonial nations like Egypt and spread to autocracies, including Russia’s seizure of Western firms. Mulder argues the 2000s globalization era was an anomaly, leaving vast assets vulnerable again.

item.title: Uganda school investigates orange-linked deaths of four girls
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Oranges investigated after four girls die in suspected Uganda school poisoning
Ugandan police are investigating the deaths of four girls aged nine to 11 at Ta'aliim Primary School in Kampala, suspecting poisoning. Three died at home, one while receiving hospital treatment. The head teacher was arrested. Eight pupils ate oranges shared by a classmate, with five experiencing vomiting; four later died. Post-mortem exams are pending to determine causes. Police are examining the village where the oranges originated and have cordoned off the school as a crime scene. Parents shared videos of their children’s final moments, accusing the school of delayed information. Authorities offered condolences and promised further updates. The incident follows previous cases of suspected contaminated food in Ugandan schools, prompting calls for improved safety measures and oversight of feeding programs.

item.title: European Leaders Reject Russia's Security Overhaul Push
item.description:
Source: FT News Feed Original headline: European leaders reject Russian push to overhaul continent’s security
European leaders have rejected Russia's proposal to overhaul the continent's security architecture, as part of ongoing Ukraine peace talks. Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that U.S. and Russian discussions on security guarantees could lead to a new European-Russia framework, which he called 'strange.' Russian officials, including foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov, demanded a ban on NATO expansion, military drills near Russia's borders, and troop withdrawals from NATO's eastern flank, framing these as necessary to restore a 'non-nuclear security' system. European Council president António Costa criticized Russia's invasion of Ukraine as the reason the existing security structure collapsed. Kaja Kallas, EU chief diplomat, argued that talks on European security should only begin after a peace deal in Ukraine. Leaders expressed concern that engaging in broader security discussions would grant Russia undue influence over NATO sovereignty. The debate over European representation in negotiations continues as leaders seek a unified stance ahead of upcoming meetings in Dublin.

item.title: Africa’s solar revolution is vast and speedy
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Middle East & Africa
Africa’s solar revolution is expanding rapidly, with Zimbabwe leading the charge. Data from Ember and Africa Tech Futures Lab estimates Zimbabwe added 948MW of solar capacity since 2023, equivalent to a third of its previous grid capacity. The continent aims to install 17GW of solar by 2026, with installations doubling in 19 countries and rising six-fold in the DRC. Most solar is distributed, installed by businesses frustrated with unreliable grids, not just utility-scale projects. In Zimbabwe, mines, farms, and villages use solar, while the UN supports mini-grids. Despite growth, challenges persist: finance remains tough, with a $6m fund deployed so far, and grid reliability issues drive customers to abandon utilities. Utilities face a 'death spiral' as large users exit, as seen in Pakistan and South Africa. Zimbabwe’s state company encourages private solar sales into the grid. In Harare’s informal settlements, residents rely on multiple power sources, including solar panels, generators, and the grid. Isaiah Nyakusendwa notes a 'solar explosion' driven by falling costs, now under 20 cents per watt, though some systems have failed. Joshua Smyth highlights the role of power cuts in spurring solar adoption, with Zimbabwe’s grid improving but tariffs rising, pushing more users toward off-grid solutions.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Sydney Designers Host Lavish Seafood Feast
item.description:
Source: FT World Original headline: How to host a seafood feast — Sydney style
Patrick and Tamsin Johnson host a relaxed seafood lunch in Darling Point, Sydney. The menu features oysters, prawns, crayfish, roast ribeye, salads, and pavlova. They source ingredients from Sydney fish markets, starting with oysters from Coffin Bay. Guests include designers, investors, and influencers. Drinks cater to individual preferences, including sticky wine, Koshihikari Echigo rice beer, and Belvedere vodka. Decor is simple, with white tablecloths, mixed roses, and candles. The couple emphasizes a slow, informal atmosphere with jazz and Grateful Dead music. Tamsin notes their approach to hosting is shaped by guests, avoiding overly formal settings. Patrick collects Joe Colombo Smoke glasses for drinks. The event extends into the evening, reflecting their signature style of effortless, curated gatherings.

item.title: AI industry's financial viability questioned as valuations strain markets
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Briefing Original headline: Can the AI boom make enough money to sustain itself?
Anthropic, the first major AI developer to go public, aims for a $1.5trn valuation, making it one of the world's largest companies. The IPO comes amid market uncertainty, with concerns over data-center debt, political shifts, and Nvidia’s leadership scandal. Analysts estimate AI needs $3trn in revenue by 2030 to justify planned data-center investments, a fraction of global wages. Current AI revenues total around $200bn, with Anthropic and OpenAI generating $81bn and $50bn annually, respectively. However, revenue growth has slowed from 80-90% to 12%, raising doubts about sustaining the boom. While AI has transformed software engineering and boosted margins for tech giants, broader economic impacts remain limited. Companies like Goldman Sachs are scaling back AI adoption due to mixed returns, while others, like JPMorgan, continue investing. The industry faces a critical test as public market scrutiny intensifies, with valuations now tied to long-term profitability rather than speculative optimism.

item.title: China Uses Romantic Relationships in Spy Operations
item.description:
Source: NYT World News Original headline: In China’s Spy Operations, Romance Can Be a Long Game
China’s intelligence services have used romantic relationships to recruit or extract information from targets for decades. American officials allege that the Ministry of State Security recruited a Chinese businesswoman to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang, with whom she had an affair. The U.S. claims Huang was unaware she was a spy, while China denies espionage allegations. Similar tactics include a Peking Opera singer’s two-decade relationship with a French diplomat, leading to espionage convictions, and a U.S. congressman’s affair with a suspected spy. U.S. officials warn against romantic ties with Chinese citizens, citing risks of manipulation. Experts note China’s approach emphasizes long-term relationships, sometimes marriages, to gain access to targets. Unlike Western agencies, China often uses coercion and blackmail, including sexual enticement. Former intelligence officers describe how Chinese operatives may stage romantic encounters to exploit emotional vulnerabilities. While such cases are rare, they highlight China’s strategy of leveraging personal connections to influence or extract information from elites. The U.S. and China both acknowledge the threat of emotional manipulation, with China advising citizens to be wary of suspicious advances.

item.title: Turkey Challenges Seabed Cable Project Amid Maritime Disputes
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Original headline: The Coming Era of Undersea Anarchy
Turkey is challenging the installation of the Great Sea Interconnector, a seabed power cable linking Greece and Cyprus, by asserting control over the project's route through Turkish waters. The dispute highlights a broader erosion of international maritime law, as Turkey, a persistent objector to UNCLOS, seeks to expand its exclusive economic zone claims in the Eastern Mediterranean. Turkey’s foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, warned against disrupting the status quo, which he argues threatens regional stability. The project, backed by the EU since 2021, faces legal hurdles as Turkey demands written notice for activities and may block installation without consent. Similar disputes involve China’s South China Sea claims, Russia’s shadow fleet, and the U.S. violating UNCLOS by permitting unilateral mining. Turkey’s actions reflect a trend of maritime anarchy, where nations prioritize national interests over international agreements. The GSI’s fate underscores the growing conflict over seabed control, with Turkey arguing that claiming the seabed grants dominance over the waters above. Other nations, including Libya and parts of the U.S., have also disregarded UNCLOS principles, signaling a shift toward unregulated maritime expansion.

item.title: Australian Teen Found Alive After Six Days in Remote Bushland
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: Australian Teen Rescued After Six Days in Remote Bushland
A 17-year-old boy missing for six days in dense bushland was found alive after an extensive search. William disappeared during a camping trip in Victoria's southeastern region, 180 km east of Melbourne. Authorities feared extreme cold temperatures would endanger him, prompting a multi-agency operation with police dogs, divers, and helicopters. Rescuers located him on Thursday morning near Stoney Creek, spotting a fishing tackle box before finding him sleeping on a rock in a dry riverbed. He was winched to safety, fed a doughnut, and taken to hospital for a checkup. His mother, Elizabeth Barkley, described him as 'in perfect health' with 'only a few scratches,' though she joked he would be 'grounded for life.' Police highlighted the rarity of such rescues, noting William had fallen into a riverbed two days prior and remained there hoping to be found. His friend had alerted authorities after William failed to return from retrieving equipment, triggering the search. Officials emphasized his resilience after enduring harsh conditions.

item.title: Kennedy Center Switches to Ticketmaster Amid Conflict of Interest Concerns
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: Kennedy Center plans Ticketmaster switch, raising conflict of interest concerns
Kennedy Center plans to switch ticketing platforms to Ticketmaster, sparking conflict of interest concerns. Richard Grenell, the center's former president, was paid $260,205 and received 102 shares of Live Nation stock while serving on the company's board, which owns Ticketmaster. Grenell was also paid nothing as Kennedy Center president. Current and former staff say the delay in ticket availability stems from the platform switch, which was negotiated while Grenell held his Live Nation role. Professor Richard Briffault called Grenell's dual positions a 'literal conflict of interest.' The Kennedy Center declined to comment on the arrangement or the switch, citing standard procurement processes. Staff members, including a former senior executive, claim Ticketmaster was never seriously considered in 2024. The center also laid off unionized box office workers after closing its main building for Trump's renovation. Ticketmaster faces criticism for fees and market dominance, while the Kennedy Center's new leadership, including artistic director Rick Canny, now oversees ticketing decisions. Canny, who previously worked with rock acts, claimed unions blocked the Ticketmaster switch in an email to the center's CFO.

item.title: Investors shift from AI hardware to India's AI services sector
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Finance & Economics Original headline: Where to find the anti-AI trade
Indian equities outperformed global markets as investors shifted away from AI hardware toward AI-related services. The Nifty 50 rose over 10% in a month, outperforming Asia's markets amid concerns about an AI bubble. Tech stocks like Infosys and Wipro surged 28% since July, while AI hardware stocks fell. Foreign investors poured $1.6bn into Indian markets on November 5th, the most since 2021, reversing a $30bn outflow trend. Lower oil prices and potential tax changes boosted the rupee and bond yields. Analysts noted sentiment shifted from excessive pessimism about Indian IT firms to optimism about coders using AI tools. The Muhurat session on Diwali saw a slight market decline, but AI stocks rallied the next day. Indian assets benefited from oil price drops and geopolitical bets on Trump-Iran talks. The Nifty 50 traded at its cheapest price-to-earnings ratio in a decade by October's end.

item.title: Jordan Faces Jihadism Resurgence Amid Violence and Repression
item.description:
Source: The Economist - Middle East & Africa Original headline: Jordan is worried about a resurgence in jihadism
Jordan faces fears of jihadism resurgence after a church attack in Karak killed nine and wounded dozens. Gunmen, linked to Islamic State, targeted mourners during a funeral procession. King Abdullah vowed revenge, ordering airstrikes in Syria, but Western diplomats suggest the move aimed to divert attention from Jordan’s domestic failures. The attack followed the killing of a Muslim policeman guarding the Sri Lankan embassy, sparking concerns about violent fundamentalism’s return. Jordan’s previous stability, bolstered by repression like banning protests and mass executions, may have fueled underground radicalization. Historical ties to Islamic State, Syria’s al-Qaeda-linked president, and regional tensions with Iran complicate the situation. While Jordan’s economy benefits from increased trade via Aqaba, public anger grows over rising fuel prices and Iranian missile attacks. Critics argue repression drives extremism underground, making it harder to control. A veteran of the Muslim Brothers warns Jordan’s role in the Iran war is unpopular, risking further unrest.

item.title: Can green cement decarbonise the data centre building boom?
item.description:
Source: FT World
Meta has committed to purchase 180,000 tonnes of low-carbon cement from Sublime Systems through environmental attribute certificates, aiming to reduce emissions from its data centre construction. The cement industry accounts for 7% of global CO₂ emissions due to fossil fuel use and limestone processing. Sublime’s electrochemical method produces 70-80% less CO₂ than traditional cement, costing $160-$180 per tonne. Meta’s agreement allows it to claim emissions reductions without using physical cement, a practice critics say enables greenwashing. Sublime argues the deal funds genuine low-carbon production, not just shifting emissions. The company plans a 150,000-200,000 tonne plant, with expansion to 1 million tonnes annually, facing challenges like volatile electricity costs. Meta’s move follows Microsoft’s 2025 deal for similar certificates. Sublime targets broader construction sectors like schools and hospitals long-term, beyond data centres. Critics warn of double-counting risks with certificates, while Sublime emphasizes its technology’s commercial viability despite testing by major cement firms.
